none_means: No qualifying prior reference verified; not a proof of novelty.

problem_class.label: nonconvex
problem_class.details: The objective is the population loss f(x) = E[ℓω(x)] on a second-countable real Hilbert space. Both the sample losses and their expectation may be nonconvex. The public inputs include the initial point x₀, the common smoothness bound L > 0, the bound Δ ≥ 0 on f(x₀), and the target ε > 0.
problem_class.evidence: LongTails/Setups/NonnegativeSmoothSampleLoss.lean, Params and spec.{Public, publicInput, valid, admissible}

oracle.label: stochastic_gradient
oracle.details: One call at (x,y) returns (∇ℓω(x), ∇ℓω(y)) for the same hidden sample ω. Calls use independent draws from a common hidden law. The reply contains only the two gradients, and the cost counts each pair as one call.

distinctive_assumptions.label: other
distinctive_assumptions.details: Every sample loss is globally nonnegative and has an L-Lipschitz gradient. These assumptions imply ‖∇ℓω(x)‖² ≤ 2Lℓω(x), so the gradient second moment is bounded by 2Lf(x) at each x and by 2LΔ at initialization. This bound can grow with the objective value. Individual samples may have different minimizers.
distinctive_assumptions.evidence: LongTails/Setups/NonnegativeSmoothSampleLoss.lean, spec.admissible, clauses for nonnegativity, HasGradientAt, the sample-gradient Lipschitz bound, the expectation defining f, and f(x₀) ≤ Δ

accuracy.label: gradient_norm
accuracy.details: The algorithm returns a measurable point X in the Hilbert space. Its population-gradient norm must be integrable and satisfy E[‖∇f(X)‖] ≤ ε.

accuracy.label: expected
accuracy.details: The expectation averages over both the algorithm seed and the independent oracle sample stream under a fixed cap on paired calls.

setup_category.label: non_standard
setup_category.reason: The formulation combines same-sample gradient pairs with a loss-dependent noise bound derived from sample nonnegativity and smoothness. The public initial-loss bound controls the initial noise scale while allowing variance to grow elsewhere.
